questions.prompt: Which header field must a client send in every HTTP/1.1 request message?

options.text: Host
User-Agent
Accept
Referer

questions.explanation: RFC 9112 requires a client to send a `Host` header field in all HTTP/1.1 request messages so the server can identify the target authority. User-Agent, Accept and Referer are useful but not required.

questions.prompt: The `Content-Type` header field indicates the media type of the associated representation, for example `application/json`.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: RFC 9110 defines `Content-Type` as the field that indicates the media type of the associated representation, which tells the recipient how to interpret the content. Compression is described separately by `Content-Encoding`.

questions.prompt: A response carries `Cache-Control: no-cache` with no field names. What does RFC 9111 require of a cache?

options.text: It must not use the stored response for a later request without first validating it successfully with the origin server
It must not store any part of the request or the response
It may reuse the response without validation until it becomes stale
It may store the response only in a private cache, never in a shared cache

questions.explanation: The unqualified `no-cache` response directive allows storing but forbids reuse without forwarding the request for validation and getting a successful response. Forbidding storage is what `no-store` does, and limiting caching to private caches is what `private` does.

questions.prompt: A client sends `GET /items/7` with `If-None-Match: "v3"`, and the current representation of that resource has the entity tag `"v3"`. According to RFC 9110, how should the origin server respond?

options.text: 304 Not Modified, without sending the representation again
412 Precondition Failed
200 OK with the full representation
409 Conflict

questions.explanation: The entity tag matches, so the `If-None-Match` condition is false. For GET or HEAD, the origin server must not perform the method and responds with 304 Not Modified. A 412 response is for other methods, for example a PUT with `If-None-Match: *` when the resource already exists.

questions.prompt: A cacheable response includes `Vary: Accept-Encoding`. How must a cache treat this stored response?

options.text: Reuse it without revalidation only for requests whose Accept-Encoding matches the original request
Never store it, because it depends on request headers
Reuse it for any request to the same URI, whatever its Accept-Encoding value
Remove the Content-Encoding before serving it to other clients

questions.explanation: Vary names request fields that may have influenced the selected response, and RFC 9111 forbids reusing the stored response without revalidation unless those fields match the original request. In effect, Vary adds those fields to the cache key; it does not make the response uncacheable.

questions.prompt: In HTTP/1.1, what is the key difference between `Content-Encoding: gzip` and `Transfer-Encoding: gzip`?

options.text: Content-Encoding is a property of the representation; Transfer-Encoding is a property of the message as it is transferred
They are synonyms, and a sender may use either one for the same purpose
Content-Encoding is hop-by-hop, while Transfer-Encoding is end-to-end
Content-Encoding applies only to request bodies, while Transfer-Encoding applies only to response bodies

questions.explanation: RFC 9112 states that, unlike Content-Encoding, Transfer-Encoding is a property of the message, not of the representation. Any recipient along the request/response chain may decode the received transfer codings or apply additional ones, as long as it updates the Transfer-Encoding field. A content coding such as gzip is instead a characteristic of the representation itself, and RFC 9110 notes that the representation is typically decoded only just before it is rendered or used.

questions.prompt: In HTTP/1.1, a connection persists after the current response by default, unless the `close` connection option is present, for example `Connection: close`.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: RFC 9112 says HTTP/1.1 defaults to persistent connections, so several requests and responses can share one connection. Persistence ends when the most recently received message carries the `close` connection option.

questions.prompt: A server sends `Set-Cookie: sid=abc; Expires=Thu, 21 Oct 2027 07:00:00 GMT; Max-Age=60` about a year before that date. Under RFC 6265, when does the cookie expire?

options.text: About 60 seconds after it is received
On 21 October 2027, as given by Expires
When the browser session ends, because the two attributes conflict
Never, because the user agent rejects the conflicting cookie

questions.explanation: RFC 6265 states that when a cookie has both Max-Age and Expires, Max-Age has precedence and controls the expiration date. Expires is effectively ignored, so the cookie expires about 60 seconds after it is received.
